title: A Reference-Less CDR Using SAR-Based Frequency-Acquisition Technique Achieving 55ns Constant Band-Searching Time and up to 63.64Gb/s/µs Acquisition Speed
problem: Reference-less CDR circuits used in burst-traffic systems suffer slow frequency acquisition (FA), which is the primary bottleneck for link wake-up latency. Dynamic data-center traffic requires frequent sleep-to-wake transitions; existing CDRs have multi-microsecond FA times that dominate link setup delay.
motivation: Network interfaces with dynamic traffic management need reference-less CDRs with minimal wake-up latency to maximize bandwidth utilization and reduce power waste from frequent mode transitions.
method: This circuit recovers timing and data from incoming signals without an external reference clock. A successive-approximation register (SAR—a circuit that uses binary search, repeatedly halving the frequency range to find the target) locks onto the correct frequency band in a constant 55 nanoseconds. A charge pump with positive net current then accelerates the final frequency tuning. These combined SAR band-switching and tuning steps complete frequency acquisition in under 150 nanoseconds.
key_novelty: Using successive-approximation register (SAR) for frequency-band selection in reference-less clock-recovery circuits guarantees constant-time frequency acquisition.
contributions: 55ns constant band-switching time via SAR architecture
Total FA time <150ns (4× faster than comparable work)
Positive-net-current charge pump enabling fast frequency convergence

metrics.other: 55ns band-search time, <150ns total FA time, 63.64Gb/s/µs acquisition speed

baselines: Conventional reference-less CDR architectures (>600ns FA time)
limitations: Not discussed; jitter performance, power consumption, and robustness to extreme temperature/voltage corners not characterized.
primary_theme: Fast SAR-based reference-less CDR for burst traffic
